metadata.title: Special Profit-Sharing Agreements
metadata.description: Handle equal divisions, capital-based portions, and charitable deductions before allocating the remainder.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Translate an agreement into ordered pools: first remove a charity percentage or management allowance if specified; divide an equal portion equally; then allocate the remaining portion by capital or capital-time weights. Keep percentages based on the stated total unless the wording defines another base. Include mixed equal-and-proportional distributions, return on capital, and a check that every pool is allocated exactly once. Ground in objective patterns 7, 30–32, and 56.

content.text: Special Profit-Sharing Agreements: Handle equal divisions, capital-based portions, and charitable deductions before allocating the remainder. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Special Profit-Sharing Agreements asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Handle equal divisions, capital-based portions, and charitable deductions before allocating the remainder. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. Some agreements divide profit in stages, such as a common equal portion and a remainder based on investment. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

Translate the agreement into separate pools. Apply charity or a prior allowance first, split any equal pool, then allocate the remaining pool by capital-time ratio. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: For ₹10,000 profit, a 5% charity deduction leaves ₹9,500. If 20% of that balance is shared equally by two partners, each first receives ₹950; allocate the remaining ₹7,600 by the agreed ratio. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Draw a pool-flow diagram before assigning any amounts. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Check that charity, equal shares, and proportional shares together use the full original profit exactly once. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Percentages may refer to the original total or to a remaining balance. Follow the exact stated base at each stage. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. “Interest on capital” in these questions means a specified portion allocated by capital unless a rate/time calculation is explicitly stated. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for special profit-sharing agreements without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
